newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-TIGER BURNING BRIGHT IN EUROPEAN MINDS.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-TIGER BURNING BRIGHT IN EUROPEAN MINDS.

text.p: How to hold that Tiger was the main question preoccupying the minds of Europe's leading golfers on Wednesday as they prepared for the Benson and Hedges International.

Not that American Tiger Woods will be playing in the tournament which starts on Thursday but such has been his impact on the game with his runaway win in the U.S. Masters that he figures large in the consciousness of all the professional players.
A larger ball was the suggestion of Europe's Ryder Cup captain Severiano Ballesteros.

"I'd rather see them change the ball instead of the golf course," the Spaniard said. "In days of new clubs and so on, I think they should change the ball like they did in 1971 or 1972 from small to big ball. I think they should take one more step and make it bigger. Certainly, it would take some length away."
Two of Europe's leading players, Briton Colin Montgomerie and German Bernhard Langer, said more fairway hazards were a way to curtail the long-hitting Woods.
"I think they should build more Tiger bunkers and Tiger water hazards," said Langer, winner of the Italian Open last weekend.
"What I mean by that is put some bunkers at 270, 300 yards, that kind of thing. The bunkers they have are from 240 to 260 and he can clear all of them."

Asked about a change in the size of the ball, Langer commented: "I don't know. I hear of one that goes only 60 percent of what it shoud. You could make everyone use that but I don't think it's the tradition of golf.
"People come out to see the ball go far. If you take that away you take away the fun and excitement. People thrive on watching John Daly and Tiger hitting the ball out of this world."

Mongomerie, the European Tour leading player for the past four years whose hopes of a possible second place in the Masters disappeared with final round 81, said: "It was slightly humiliating, I suppose, what Tiger did. All credit to him. It was a fantastic performance."
He also suggested making golf courses tougher. "I think the days of golf courses with no rough are over. I would like to see some rough.
"There's got to be more trouble, if you like, where one guy can't come up and win in such an efficient manner, I'd like to see greens softer, more receptive, and have some rough."

Asked if he thought that would stop Woods, Montgomerie replied: "It would make a more level playing field, although people say if he's that good why level it out. That's their decision, not mine. Tiger at Troon (in Scotland) or Tiger anywhere is a threat."

But Montgomerie was unstinting in his praise for the 21-year-old American who turned professional only last year. "I witnessed his mental attitude and the way he handled everything. I witnessed a 65 and have never seen one scored so easily round a course in my life. You've got to praise that.
"What I witnessed was something a little bit different."
